chapter_theme: Three songs at Vedaranyam (வேதாரணியம், Vedavanam): pleas against the bond of deeds, disease and lust, and against the women whose eyes conquer the land, with praise that dwells on Rama's story as the deeds of Murugan's uncle.
structure_note: 840 and 841 share their closing lines, naming Tiruttani, Senthil, Palani and Vedavanam; both praise Rama at length. 839 is a short song.

839.reading: The poet asks whether he, a poor man who has not thought of the Lord as a companion in his karmic bond, his sorrow, long disease and wasting lust, must wander daily in griefs, and asks Murugan to remove his faults and give him thought of the red feet. The praise names the dark-cloud uncle who bridged the sea and conquered Lanka, the younger brother of the elephant-faced one, and the son given by Sankara of Vedavanam.
839.nuance: சோரம் இதற்குச் சிந்தை நினைந்துறு துணையாதே: the failure confessed is not to have taken the Lord as companion (துணை) in distress. The line on Rama's seven days at Lanka is hard to read.

840.reading: The poet describes women who walk in fine sarees, loosen and tie their garlands, comb their hair, speak sweeter than honey, imprison lustful men and conquer every land with their eyes, and asks whether he must fall into their evening bewilderment, sink into the arts of love and wander in pain; he asks for the grace of feet like the young sun's rays that end maya. The praise tells Rama's story: the walk through the wilderness, the dark rakshasi defeated, seven trees pierced with one arrow, Vali's chest torn, the sea bridged at Varuna's word, Lanka destroyed and grace given to Vibhishana, Murugan's uncle, and names Tiruttani, Senthil, Palani and Vedavanam.
840.nuance: மாலை மயக்கு can mean the bewilderment of the garland or of evening; both suit a street scene at dusk. The feet are likened to the rays of the young sun (வால ரவிக் கிரணங்கள்) that dispel maya, light against darkness.

841.reading: The poet lists the women who lure with thread-thin waists, anklets, Meru-like breasts and fish eyes, and asks whether, plunging into the sea of pleasure on their honey lips, giving up all virtue and sunk in lust, he must wander having lost the tapas that brings clarity. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva who wears the crescent, thumbai, the river, konrai, karanthai and Vasuki, and the nephew of Mukunda, who measured Mahabali's world with a step and cut the ten heads and twenty arms of Lanka's king.
841.nuance: சீலம் அனைத்தும் ஒழிந்து ... தேறு தவத்தை இழந்து: the loss named is of conduct and of tapas, not only of wealth or health. The closing two lines repeat 840's word for word.

links.note: The two songs share their last lines and their Rama praise; 840 asks for the feet that end maya, while 841 only asks whether it must lose its tapas, so the pair shows one shrine-formula carrying two pleas.
